proposal.original_claim_summary: The card states DOGE closed at least 10 Social Security field offices by February 2025 and forced disabled and elderly beneficiaries into long trips, using White Plains as an example.

identified_problems.explanation: SSA stated on March 27, 2025 that it had not permanently closed or announced the closure of any local field office since January 1; it had announced one permanent hearing-office closure in White Plains.
The sites identified for lease termination were described by SSA primarily as small hearing rooms with no assigned employees, not at least 10 local field offices.

SSA later said the White Plains hearing-office closure had been chosen by the prior administration in December 2024, undercutting the card's attribution of that closure to DOGE beginning in February 2025.

proposal.proposed_title: SSA Reviews Underused Leases; White Plains Hearing Office Closure Draws Access Concerns
proposal.proposed_synopsis: SSA said on March 27, 2025 that it had not permanently closed or announced the permanent closure of any local field office since January 1. It had announced the closure of one hearing office in White Plains, New York, and said most sites sent to GSA for possible lease termination were small hearing rooms with no assigned employees. A later SSA release said the White Plains closure decision dated to December 2024. The stored claim that DOGE had already closed at least 10 Social Security field offices is not supported.

frozen_original.title: DOGE Closed Social Security Offices, Left Disabled Facing 135-Mile Trips
frozen_original.synopsis: By February 2025, DOGE began closing at least 10 Social Security field offices, including the White Plains, NY hearing office serving seven counties with 2,000 pending cases. Closure would force elderly and disabled beneficiaries to travel up to 135 miles to the next office, potentially into another state. SSA staffing was already at a 50-year low when DOGE arrived, and ProPublica reported many closures targeted low-income, disabled, and orphaned recipients with no internet access.

frozen_original.title: Trump Threatens to Arrest Former Officials Who Criticized Him — Milley, Esper
frozen_original.synopsis: Trump and senior White House officials made public statements in February 2025 threatening the arrest and prosecution of former officials who had publicly criticized Trump, specifically naming retired General Mark Milley and former Defense Secretary Mark Esper. Both men had written memoirs and given interviews describing Trump as dangerous and unfit for command. The threats were widely seen as an attempt to silence critics and warn current officials against speaking out. Civil liberties lawyers noted that arrest for political speech would violate the First Amendment and constitute a textbook authoritarian abuse of law enforcement. Milley and Esper both publicly stated they would not be intimidated.

proposal.original_claim_summary: Trump Threatens to Revoke Tax-Exempt Status of Universities That Don't Comply
proposal.original_synopsis: In February 2025, Trump posted on Truth Social threatening to revoke the tax-exempt status of universities that refused to comply with his administration's demands on DEI, protest policies, and faculty governance — a threat that, if carried out, would expose elite university endowments worth tens of billions of dollars to taxation and potentially devastate research and scholarship programs. Legal scholars noted such revocations require IRS action and would face enormous legal hurdles, and that threatening tax status to coerce ideological compliance raised serious First Amendment violations. Nevertheless, the threat sent shockwaves through higher education, with university boards convening emergency legal reviews. The IRS's independence from presidential political pressure was already under assault as the administration sought to use tax enforcement as a tool of political intimidation.

proposal.original_claim_summary: Trump signs order allowing indefinite detention without charge for immigrants

identified_problems.explanation: The January 20 order directs detention of removable aliens pending removal proceedings or removal 'to the extent permitted by law'; it does not authorize indefinite detention without charge or categorically eliminate bail hearings.
The synopsis claims immediate judicial blocks of this supposed order, but the described indefinite-detention provision is not present in the order.

proposal.proposed_synopsis: Hide the indefinite-detention card. Trump's January 20 immigration order called for detention pending removal proceedings or removal to the extent permitted by law, which is materially different from an order authorizing indefinite detention without charges.

claims.claim: The January 20 order directed detention pending removal proceedings or removal to the extent permitted by law.

frozen_original.title: Trump signs order allowing indefinite detention without charge for immigrants
frozen_original.synopsis: Trump signed an executive order authorizing the indefinite detention of immigrants without filing charges, violating due process protections and fundamental constitutional rights. The order directed immigration judges to deny bail hearings and allowed ICE to hold individuals indefinitely while immigration courts remained backlogged. Federal judges immediately moved to block the order, ruling that even non-citizens have due process rights under the Fifth Amendment. The order was part of a systematic effort to eliminate judicial oversight of immigration enforcement.
